The maximum total length attained by Japanese jack mackerel (Trachurus japonicus) has been documented at 50 cm [Li = 50 cm], a size consistent with the upper range reported for carangids of the genus Trachurus. Females in this species reach puberty at a total length of 19 cm [Lp = 19 cm], a metric derived from extensive gonadal surveys conducted across the East China Sea during the spawning season. This length-based threshold for reproductive maturation corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 67.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 67.3 grams], suggesting that individuals allocate substantial somatic growth to reaching a critical body size before initiating vitellogenesis. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a power-law function typical of pelagic teleosts, with females investing considerably in trunk musculature to support sustained swimming during their extensive foraging migrations. Comparative data from other Trachurus species indicate that the length at first reproduction is generally lower in warmer waters, though the values for Japanese jack mackerel in temperate regions around Kyushu appear to represent a stable population-level trait.

At the other end of the life-history spectrum, the ultimate wet weight recorded for adults of Trachurus japonicus reaches approximately 1.2 kilograms [Wwi = approximately 1.2 kilograms], a value derived from morphometric equations linking total length to eviscerated mass in landed catches. This maximum body mass, representing the heaviest individuals sampled from commercial fisheries over multiple years, is attained primarily by older females that have completed numerous spawning seasons. By contrast, the wet weight at birth is remarkably low, with newly hatched yolk-sac larvae weighing only 0.000278 grams [Wwb = 0.000278 grams] based on an egg diameter of approximately 0.81 mm, a value interpolated from egg size data reported for the congener Trachurus mediterraneus. This minute starting mass reflects the pelagic egg strategy common among carangids, wherein females produce large numbers of small, buoyant eggs that undergo rapid embryonic development in the surface layer. The contrast between neonatal and adult body mass, spanning nearly seven orders of magnitude in wet weight, underscores the extreme growth trajectory that defines the early life stages of this commercially important species.

Laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable water temperature of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C] have yielded precise estimates for several early-life developmental rates. Under these thermal conditions, the age at birth, defined as the time elapsed from fertilisation to chorion rupture, was recorded at 13 days [ab = 13 days], a duration that reflects the relatively slow metabolic pace imposed by cool temperate waters at a temperature of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C]. The same experimental conditions also provided data on the maximum reproductive rate: females produced on average 410,400 eggs per batch [N_R_i = 410,400 eggs per batch], spawning on a daily basis during the peak of the season [F_R_i = spawning on a daily basis during the peak of the season]. This extraordinarily high fecundity, sustained over many consecutive days, is characteristic of batch-spawning pelagic teleosts that rely on numerical output rather than parental investment to ensure recruitment success. The daily spawning frequency observed at this temperature is among the highest recorded for any carangid, suggesting that the species has evolved a life-history strategy that maximises offspring production during brief windows of favourable oceanographic conditions in the Kuroshio Current region.

Longevity estimates for Trachurus japonicus in the same thermal regime of 13.8 °C [T = 13.8 °C] indicate a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years], equivalent to approximately 4,380 days. This lifespan was determined through otolith increment analysis of the oldest individuals captured in the Sea of Japan, where slow growth and delayed senescence characterise populations at the cooler northern edge of the species' distribution. Historical tag-recapture studies corroborate this figure, with several recaptures occurring more than a decade after initial marking. The life span is comparable to that of other temperate carangids, such as Trachurus trachurus in the Northeast Atlantic, though Japanese jack mackerel appears to reach terminal size somewhat earlier relative to its total longevity. The combination of a 12-year lifespan and early maturation at 19 cm total length implies a relatively short generation time for a fish of its ultimate size, a demographic pattern that confers resilience to moderate fishing pressure but makes the species vulnerable to recruitment overfishing during prolonged environmental perturbations.

Asymptotic growth in this carangid typically saturates before the species attains its documented ceiling of 50 cm [Li = 50 cm]. Individuals from the Pacific side of the Japanese archipelago tend to reach the pubertal length of 19 cm [Lp = 19 cm] more rapidly than their Sea of Japan counterparts, likely due to differences in prey availability and water temperature. The ultimate wet weight of older females, which can approach 1.2 kilograms [Wwi = 1.2 kilograms], represents a substantial energetic investment in gonadal tissue during the protracted spawning season from February to June. Field surveys using plankton nets indicate that newly emerged larvae, weighing just 0.000278 grams [Wwb = 0.000278 grams], begin exogenous feeding within days of hatching, transitioning rapidly from yolk dependence to active predation on copepod nauplii. The wet weight at puberty of 67.3 grams [Wwp = 67.3 grams] corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis in histological samples, marking a critical life-history transition that is tightly coupled to both seasonal temperature cycles and individual energy reserves accumulated during the preceding winter.
